analysis.one_liner: Gives domestic violence survivors paid job-protected leave, unemployment benefits, and insurance protections.
analysis.headline: A bill to give survivors of domestic violence and sexual assault time off to get safe, protection from being fired, and unemployment benefits died in committee without a hearing or vote, despite 71 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require employers with 15 or more workers to give up to 30 days of leave per year — up to 56 hours of it paid — to survivors of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, or stalking, so they can get medical care, go to court, relocate, or plan for their safety, with their job and health coverage protected. It would bar employers from firing or punishing someone for being a survivor or for seeking help, would stop states from denying unemployment benefits to people who leave a job because of the violence, and would stop insurers from denying, canceling, or surcharging coverage because someone is a survivor. It would also reauthorize federal grants that help workplaces assist survivors.
analysis.who_benefits: Survivors of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking — and their family members. Nearly half of sexual assault survivors lose or quit their jobs afterward, and the bill's stated aim is economic independence, which research shows is one of the best predictors of whether a survivor can escape an abuser. Workers at employers with 15 or more employees would get protected time off, a right to safety accommodations at work, and a path to unemployment benefits if violence forces them out of a job. Survivors would also gain protection from insurers refusing, canceling, or surcharging their policies and from insurers disclosing abuse information.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Domestic violence and sexual assault survivors

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers with 15 or more employees to provide up to 30 days of 'safe leave' in a 12-month period for survivors to seek medical care, counseling, shelter, safety planning, relocation, or legal help, including not less than one hour of earned paid leave per 30 hours worked, capped at 56 paid hours a year.

Guarantees return to the same or an equivalent job after leave, keeps health coverage in place during leave, and keeps all survivor-related information confidential, including barring employers from demanding details of the abuse.

Makes it illegal for employers or public assistance agencies to fire, punish, or discriminate against someone because they are a survivor, attend court proceedings, or ask for safety measures like a changed phone number, a transfer, or an adjusted schedule.

Amends federal unemployment law so compensation cannot be denied when someone leaves a job because of domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking, and states cannot add extra eligibility restrictions for survivors, with a sworn statement or a single piece of documentation enough to qualify.

Prohibits insurers from denying, refusing to renew, or canceling a policy, denying a claim, or adding a premium surcharge because an applicant is a survivor of domestic or sexual violence, and stops health plans from cutting off a survivor's coverage because it was originally in an abuser's name.

Authorizes grant funds for training unemployment and welfare caseworkers on abuse dynamics and lets states use existing welfare funds to pay expedited short-term emergency benefits to survivors taking safe leave.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees bear the cost of paid safe leave and new compliance and record-keeping duties. Insurers and employers who self-insure face restrictions on denying, canceling, or surcharging policies for survivors and on extending coverage after a divorce or separation. States must update unemployment and welfare administration and train staff, supported in part by authorized federal grants of about $12 million a year for fiscal 2019 through 2022.

drawbacks.text: The mandate puts real costs on employers: paid leave accrual (up to 56 hours per year), job restoration, continued health coverage during leave, and new enforcement rules with damages and attorney's fees for violations, applying to businesses with as few as 15 employees.

The bill's own findings acknowledge some employers would see disruption; employers may require documentation for leave and can deny job restoration to their highest-paid 10 percent of employees when returning them would cause substantial economic injury.
Most of the 30 days of leave is unpaid unless the worker uses earned paid leave or substitutes existing paid leave, so a survivor without accrued paid time may go without income during leave.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but modest and targeted: paid leave is capped at 56 hours a year, employers with existing sufficient policies are exempted, and the leave can be unpaid beyond that. The benefit side is substantial — nearly half of sexual assault survivors lose their jobs, survivors lose millions of paid work days a year, and economic independence is one of the strongest predictors of escaping an abuser. The bill is a reasonable trade for survivors' safety and job stability; the honest objection is the compliance burden it places on small and mid-sized businesses and the possibility of increased leave usage costs for low-margin employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced, none of them ever held a hearing or scheduled it, and the Congress ended without a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Lucille Roybal-Allard (D-CA) introduced the bill on October 31, 2017, joined by 17 original cosponsors.

It was referred the same day to four committees — Education and the Workforce, Financial Services, Ways and Means, and Judiciary — a referral pattern that splits a bill's provisions across committees and makes single-committee action harder.
71 Democratic members of the House cosponsored the bill; no Republicans are listed as cosponsors.
No committee reported the bill, no hearing or floor action is recorded, and the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 without the bill ever coming to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have paid for safe leave and insurers who would have faced new restrictions on denying or canceling coverage are better off, since they avoid the mandate; survivors remain without any of the federal protections the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and insurers that avoided the mandate

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every listed cosponsor was a Democrat.

against.role: House majority party of the 115th Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 71 cosponsors were Democrats, introduced during a Republican House majority; no Republican signed on and the bill never received a recorded vote, so opposition shows up as inaction rather than a roll call.

industries.note: Would bear paid safe leave costs, job-restoration and health-coverage obligations, and damages and attorney's fees for violations. Its interest in avoiding these costs runs against survivors' need for protected time off and job security.

industries.industry: Insurers (health, life, disability, property and casualty) and self-insured employers
industries.note: Barred from denying, renewing, or canceling policies, denying claims, or surcharging premiums because someone is a survivor, and required to continue coverage originally in an abuser's name. Its interest in underwriting flexibility runs against survivors' access to coverage and safety.

industries.industry: Survivor services organizations (shelters, rape crisis centers, domestic violence programs)
industries.note: Eligible for reauthorized federal resource-center grants and new training-grant funding (about $12 million a year authorized for 2019-2022), and their documentation would qualify survivors for leave and unemployment benefits.
Must update rules, train staff, and pay benefits to more claimants, but receive authorized federal grant funding for the training and can pay emergency leave benefits from existing welfare funds.
